findings.text: §12's cause evidence attributes the leak to "one run of `tests/test_cross_node_writes_refresh_the_index.py::test_an_open_stream_receives_the_added_row_and_stays_open`", which "added two `/_changes/sample` lines to the live served log (83 such lines before, 85 after)", while its own done-when records the opposite for that population: "Run alone, the single stream test leaked nothing in 6 runs, because its daemon handler dies with the process; the whole file leaked 6 such lines". Both figures cannot describe the same command, and the section's own explanation (the daemon dies with the process when the test runs alone) makes the single-test attribution the wrong one; the live log today carries 85 `/_changes/sample` lines, so the total is real, but the reproduction the Why names is not the run that produced it

findings.reason: the ordering of the over-bound state is what decides whether this control can go red, and the plan must state it (arrange the over-bound state, and lower the bound, only after the binding request) or the node's gate proves nothing.
findings.text: §12's case (2) states its precondition as "the log bound lowered for the test and the first home's log already over it" without fixing it after the binding request, but the binding request is itself served through `Handler.handle_one_request`, which calls `_bound_server_log()` (reckon/serve.py:2241) before any path is kept; if the bound is lowered and the first home's log put over it before that setup request, the setup request itself rotates the first home's log and publishes the predecessor, so the post-move request finds the fixed server's live file empty and returns False, and the case's assertion ("leaving its predecessor beside it") is satisfied by the setup rotation under the control as well — the control then passes and the case falsifies nothing
